newsitem.title: POLAND: FLOOD RECEDES IN POLAND DESPITE RAIN.
newsitem.headline: FLOOD RECEDES IN POLAND DESPITE RAIN.

text.p: Water swamping large areas in southwestern Poland receded on Saturday as rain, which had threatned to renew flood surges, proved less heavy than forecast, officials said.

"It rained here and there at night and there still are occasional showers in areas affected by the floods but on the average water levels are going down," crisis committee spokesman Krzysztof Pomes told Reuters.

He said downpours in the Czech Republic were likely to swell again the Odra river, which had scourged Poland and eastern part of Germany in three weeks of the region's worst natural disaster in centuries.
"No new floodings are expected. Stability of flood-protection dykes, which are soaked like the sponge in many places, is our main concern now," he said.
Heroic sand-bagging effort by local communities, soldiers and firemen continued along the Odra and other rivers to strengthen the dykes, he said.
The rain -- heaviest in central-eastern Poland and Warsaw, which is unaffected by the flood, is forecast to recede by Sunday, the Meteorology and Water Management Institute said.
"The forecast is optimistic, we should see the sun from Monday," an official at the institute said.
Pomes said that water had left about 300 sq km of land and 46 towns and villages since Friday. More than 2,200 sq km of land still remained under water out of more than 6,000 sq km affected in total.

Previously evacuated people were coming back to their homes, often to find debris or drowned livestock. In many places they faced the challenge of avoiding the dysentery and other illness threatened by universal filth.
More than 40,000 people were still evacuaded from their homes, Pomes said.
The flood, which has killed 55 people in Poland and paralysed several major cities including provincial capitals of Wroclaw and Opole, still affected 371 towns and villages.
The disaster, which has poisoned soil and underground waters in many places by destroying sewage plants and washing out chemical waste product dumps, has caused yet another environmental tragedy.

Some 15 tonnes of freon gas that destroys the earth's ozone layer has escaped into the atmosphere from a company in the southern city of Raciborz as a result of the flood, the crisis committee said in a statement late on Friday.
The ozone layer, thinnnig over the recent decades, protects the earth from deadly radiation from the outer space. Freon, used in cooling devices and spray cosmetics is banned in many countries.
Independent analysts estimated damages of the flood on Saturday at between five and 7.5 billion zlotys ($1.5-$2.3 billion), equivalent of 1.2-1.7 percent of gross domestic products.

The analysts of the GUS-PAN and NOBE institutes said in a report published in the Rzeczpospolita daily that the flood would slow down Poland's economic growth to between five and 5.4 percent of GDP in 1997 from six percent earlier forecast. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
